name: Serpentine Pavilion 2013
note: The lattice works less as a single enclosure than as a field of occupiable edges and changing degrees of openness.
whyRelevant: Useful when a trace is asking how one boundary or edge can support several degrees of occupation rather than one fixed room condition.
prompt: What changes if the edge becomes occupiable instead of acting only as a boundary?

name: Serpentine Pavilion 2017
note: A broad canopy and central gathering condition frame shelter as both environmental protection and collective social space.
whyRelevant: Useful when one spatial move needs to carry both climatic performance and social use.
prompt: Could one canopy condition support shelter and gathering at the same time?

name: Serpentine Pavilion 2009
note: A continuous reflective roof provides shelter while the pavilion stays visually and physically open from many sides.
whyRelevant: Useful for separating the idea of shelter from the idea of enclosure.
prompt: What if shelter remains continuous while enclosure stays minimal?

name: Serpentine Pavilion 2015
note: Multiple openings and layered circulation make arrival and route choice part of the pavilion experience.
whyRelevant: Useful when a trace is testing whether one main route is necessary or whether several entries can distribute movement.
prompt: Could several thresholds support different kinds of participation without confusing circulation?

name: Serpentine Pavilion 2021
note: The pavilion draws from places of meeting and belonging across London, using social-spatial references as design material.
whyRelevant: Useful when grounding a design move in existing social spaces rather than inventing a generic idea of community.
prompt: Which existing places already support the behaviour being sought, and what spatial qualities can be translated?

name: Serpentine Pavilion 2006
note: The ovoid canopy could be raised or lowered in response to weather, making environmental change part of the pavilion's operation.
whyRelevant: Useful when flexibility is tied to changing conditions over time rather than constant rearrangement of every element.
prompt: Could one adjustable element respond to changing conditions while the rest of the pavilion stays stable?

name: BA_LIK Pavilion
note: Five wheeled elements can be moved and connected so the pavilion shifts between compact enclosure and a looser open arrangement.
whyRelevant: Useful for testing whether physical reconfiguration needs many small movable objects or a smaller number of larger spatial components.
prompt: Would a few larger mobile components produce clearer reconfiguration than many loose pieces of furniture?

name: Timber Pavilion of the Vidy-Lausanne Theatre
note: Retractable seating changes the room between frontal, bifrontal and open configurations without requiring a completely different building.
whyRelevant: Useful when peak-period capacity and everyday openness need to coexist within the same footprint.
prompt: Could extra seating disappear into the architecture rather than becoming loose furniture that must be stored elsewhere?

name: The Dulwich Pavilion
note: Most wall panels are moveable or removable while the roof and deck remain fixed, allowing different event configurations.
whyRelevant: Useful for asking which parts of a pavilion actually need to move, and which can remain stable.
prompt: Which element needs to change for flexibility to occur: furniture, enclosure, programme, or all three?

name: Green Agora Pavilion
note: The pavilion uses a modular aluminium system to support community dialogue and everyday neighbourhood activity.
whyRelevant: Useful as a Singapore-based precedent when community use, modularity and everyday activation need to be considered together.
prompt: Can a structural system support both a spatial programme and an ongoing community activity?
